content.intro: This lesson introduces synchronizing local and remote branches as part of Remote Repositories and Synchronization. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: An upstream relationship lets Git report whether a local branch is ahead of or behind its configured remote-tracking branch. That summary can be stale until fetching updates the reference.

content_blocks.title: Remote synchronization flow
content_blocks.alt_text: Fetch transfers objects and updates remote-tracking references; integration is a separate decision; push publishes local commits if remote policy accepts them.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** An upstream relationship lets Git report whether a local branch is ahead of or behind its configured remote-tracking branch. That summary can be stale until fetching updates the reference.

For **Synchronizing Local and Remote Branches**, keep the named subtopics in view: Tracking branches; Setting upstream references; Checking ahead and behind counts; Choosing merge or rebase before pushing. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. The output depends on upstream configuration and current remote-tracking refs; fetch before trusting remote state that may be stale.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.
